summary: Defines the core schema for SCIM, the common set of attributes and resource types for things such as users and groups. The goal is to make user management in cloud applications simpler and cheaper by giving everyone a shared way to describe identities.

plainLanguage.summary: SCIM gives organizations a shared JSON structure for describing people, groups, and related identity data. Services can add fields while keeping their extensions separate from the common schema.

subtitle: A shared JSON schema for identities that can be exchanged between organizations and services.

tldr.problem: Organizations often need to manage the same people in several cloud services, each with its own data model. Separate integrations add work for both clients and service providers.
tldr.mechanism: SCIM defines JSON resources, attribute types and rules, common User and Group schemas, extension containers, and schemas that describe a service provider's capabilities.
tldr.outcome: The core schema gives clients and service providers a shared way to describe identity resources. RFC 7643 has been updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967.

today: RFC 7643 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015. It has been updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967, and has not been obsoleted. The companion protocol specification is RFC 7644.

sections.title: Why a Common Identity Schema
sections.content:
Cloud services have often used different methods to describe and manage users. Organizations connecting to several providers then need separate integration work for each one. The System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) provides a common schema and an HTTP protocol suite.

RFC 7643 defines the JSON schema and extension model for Users, Groups, and other resource types. Its companion, RFC 7644, defines how clients exchange these resources over HTTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services may describe the same person in different ways. SCIM defines shared labels and rules so identity information can move between services more consistently.

sections.title: Attributes and Data Types
sections.content:
SCIM schemas define individual attributes, including their data type, whether they hold one or many values, when they may change, and when they are returned. The eight types are string, boolean, decimal, integer, dateTime, binary, reference, and complex. A complex value contains simple sub-attributes.

Multi-valued attributes are JSON arrays. Their elements may include labels such as work or home, a primary flag, a display value, or a reference. For a given attribute, at most one value may be marked primary. An unassigned value, null, and an empty array have equivalent state.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute says what kind of value it holds and how a service may change or return it. A field can hold one answer or a list, such as several email addresses.

sections.title: Resources and Schema Extensions
sections.content:
A SCIM resource is a JSON object with a required schemas array, common attributes, core attributes, and optional extensions. The service provider assigns each resource's stable id; a provisioning client may supply an externalId. The server also supplies metadata such as resource type, creation time, last modification, location, and version.

Extensions add attributes without inheritance. Each extension's schema URI names a separate JSON container, reducing conflicts between independently defined fields. A service provider can also define a new resource type with its own endpoint and schema.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource includes a schema label and standard identification fields. Extra fields go in a container named for their extension, so they do not get confused with core fields.

sections.title: User, Group, and Enterprise Attributes
sections.content:
The User schema requires a non-empty, provider-unique userName. It also defines personal details, contact information, status, and other attributes. The password attribute is write-only: a service provider must never return its cleartext or hashed value and should hash a password it stores locally.

The Group schema requires displayName and can list User or Group members, which allows nested groups. The enterprise User extension adds attributes such as employeeNumber, costCenter, organization, division, department, and a manager reference. The schema does not define what authorization group membership grants.
sections.plainLanguage: A User resource can describe a person's account and contact details. A Group resource lists members, while the enterprise extension adds common workplace details.

sections.title: Rules Attached to Each Attribute
sections.content:
Attribute characteristics tell a service provider whether a value is required, case-sensitive, unique, mutable, or returned in responses. Mutability may be readOnly, readWrite, immutable, or writeOnly. Returned values may be always, never, default, or request. These characteristics guide how a provider handles each field.

For example, an immutable attribute may be set when a resource is created but not later changed. A writeOnly value may be updated but is never returned. The schema also describes allowed reference types and suggested canonical values.
sections.plainLanguage: Each field has rules for changing it and showing it to clients. A password can be written but not read back; a read-only value cannot be changed by a client.

sections.title: Describing a Service Provider
sections.content:
The ServiceProviderConfig schema reports supported features such as PATCH, bulk operations, filtering, sorting, version tags, password changes, and authentication schemes. Clients can use this information to learn which optional operations a provider supports.

ResourceType describes a resource's name, endpoint, base schema, and extensions. Schema describes the attributes and their characteristics. These read-only resources let a provider expose its schema and capabilities through discovery endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: A service can publish information about its supported features and resource types. Clients can read this information before choosing which operations and fields to use.

sections.title: Passwords and Personal Information
sections.content:
SCIM data is intended to travel using the SCIM protocol, so implementations also need to follow the security considerations in RFC 7644. Passwords and other credentials need special protection. Password values must not be stored in cleartext, and the RFC recommends protected storage and input validation.

The RFC treats all SCIM attributes as sensitive personal information. Clients should send only data the provider needs, and providers should limit access to authorized parties. Where possible, identifiers should be scoped to a tenant or client to reduce correlation between domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Identity records contain private information, including credentials. Share only the data a service needs and restrict who can read it.

sections.title: The SCIM Schema Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the SCIM URN sub-namespace urn:ietf:params:scim and a registry for SCIM schema URIs. A schema URI gives each schema or extension a stable name. Once allocated, a name cannot be reassigned for a different purpose.

New core and API schemas require designated-expert review and publication in an RFC. The RFC also defines when changes to schema data types or previously documented schemas require an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM schema names are recorded in a public registry. A registered name stays tied to its original purpose, so another schema cannot reuse it.
